title: Clinical characteristics and outcomes of respiratory syncytial virus and human metapneumovirus ınfections in children under five years of age

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human metapneumovirus (hMPV) are major causes of acute respiratory tract infections in young children and share many epidemiological and clinical characteristics.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study was a retrospective comparative cohort study conducted at a tertiary pediatric hospital, including children aged 1-71 months with laboratory-confirmed RSV or hMPV infection identified by multiplex real-time polymerase chain reaction. RSV cases were identified between September 2022 and April 2023, while hMPV cases were identified between September 2022 and December 2025. Both outpatient and hospitalized patients were enrolled.
analysis.methods: Children with laboratory-confirmed RSV or hMPV infection were included in the study. The infections were identified using multiplex real-time polymerase chain reaction. The study compared clinical characteristics, outcomes, and healthcare costs associated with RSV and hMPV infections in children younger than five years of age.
analysis.main_results: Children with hMPV infection were significantly older and more frequently had underlying comorbidities than those with RSV infection. Bronchiolitis, cough, nasal congestion, tachypnea, chest retractions, rhonchi, oxygen supplementation, inhaled therapies, corticosteroid use, and hospitalization were more common among children with RSV infection (all p < 0.05).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings are consistent with previous studies, highlighting differences in age distribution, clinical presentation, and healthcare utilization between RSV and hMPV infections. This study provides new insights into the distinct clinical profiles of these two viruses in young children.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results can inform targeted surveillance, diagnosis, and management strategies for hMPV infections in older children with comorbidities, as well as guide the development of more effective interventions for RSV in younger populations.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and single-center data, which may affect generalizability. However, the data provide additional evidence from a tertiary pediatric center in Türkiye and support the generalizability of these observations across different geographic settings.

analysis.summary_en: This study compares the clinical characteristics, outcomes, and healthcare costs of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human metapneumovirus (hMPV) infections in children under five years of age. Conducted as a retrospective comparative cohort study at a tertiary pediatric hospital in Türkiye, the research included 693 children, with 547 having RSV and 146 having hMPV infections. The findings reveal that hMPV predominantly affects older children with comorbidities, while RSV is more common in younger children and associated with more severe symptoms and higher healthcare utilization. These results align with previous studies and highlight the distinct clinical profiles of RSV and hMPV. The study's limitations include its retrospective nature and single-center focus, but the data support the generalizability of the findings across different geographic settings.

title: Genomic Surveillance of Human Metapneumovirus in the United States, 2010-2025.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand the genomic epidemiology of human metapneumovirus (HMPV) in the United States, addressing the need for enhanced surveillance of this understudied respiratory virus.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved genomic surveillance of HMPV-positive specimens from two cohorts: the household-based HIVE study (2010-2022) in Michigan and the multicenter IVY network (2022-2025) of hospitalized adults, totaling 616 specimens.
analysis.methods: Hybrid capture and whole-genome sequencing were performed on the specimens. Consensus sequences were generated using IRMA, clades were annotated using Nextclade, and phylogenetic trees were constructed for HMPV-A and HMPV-B using IQ-TREE and TreeTime. Selection analysis was conducted using SLAC.
analysis.main_results: Complete genomes were obtained from 325 specimens. The study revealed the continued predominance of the A2.2.2 clade and little geographic structure in the United States. Genomic diversity was highest in the glycoprotein (G) gene, with a shift from variants bearing the 180nt duplication to ones with a 111nt duplication. Phylogenetic analyses supported the duplication-deletion model for the origin of the duplications. The conserved fusion (F) protein showed limited antigenic variation and low rates of nonsynonymous substitutions.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings underscore the utility of enhanced genomic surveillance for understanding HMPV evolution and informing vaccine development. There was little genomic diversity in vaccine-targeted epitopes.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results can inform surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment of HMPV infections, as well as guide future vaccine development efforts.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the reliance on genomic surveillance and the lack of detailed clinical data. The findings suggest moderate evidence strength.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted genomic surveillance of HMPV in the United States, revealing the predominance of the A2.2.2 clade and little geographic structure. Genomic diversity was highest in the glycoprotein gene, with a shift from 180nt to 111nt duplications. The findings highlight the importance of enhanced surveillance for vaccine development.

analysis.study_design_and_population: While HMPV typically causes mild symptoms, its effects on the elderly and immunocompromised individuals prompted health authorities to emphasize preventive measures.
analysis.methods: This study focuses on the use of sentiment analysis to understand public reactions to HMPV during the 2024 outbreak. analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: This paper explores how sentiment analysis can enhance our understanding of public reactions to HMPV by analyzing data from social media platforms like YouTube.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates public reactions to Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV) during the 2024 outbreak using sentiment analysis. The research aims to understand how public sentiment varies, with some individuals expressing anxiety while others show carelessness. The study emphasizes the importance of tracking public sentiment to guide health messaging and inform policies. It applies advanced transformer models, particularly XLNet, achieving an accuracy of 93.50% in sentiment classification tasks. Additionally, the research incorporates explainable AI (XAI) through SHAP to provide transparency in how the model identifies key factors influencing public sentiment. The findings suggest that sentiment analysis can be a valuable tool for monitoring public perception of HMPV and improving communication strategies. title: Bivalent RSVpreF Effectiveness Against Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV)-Related Respiratory Disease Hospitalization and Emergency Department Visits Across Three RSV Seasons

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) protein subunit vaccines reduce the risk of severe outcomes such as hospitalization and emergency department (ED) visits for at least two RSV seasons following vaccination. No data have been published on real-world RSV vaccine effectiveness (VE) beyond the second season after vaccination.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective test-negative case-control study evaluates bivalent RSVpreF VE among adults aged ≥60 years at Kaiser Permanente Southern California, USA, with lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) or acute respiratory illness (ARI) over three RSV seasons (11/24/2023-4/18/2026).
analysis.methods: Cases were RSV-positive without coinfection. Controls were negative for RSV, hMPV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and positive for a non-vaccine preventable disease pathogen. Exposure was bivalent RSVpreF (Abrysvo) receipt ≥ 21 days before LRTD/ARI. Adjusted VE was estimated using odds ratios from multivariable logistic regression or generalized estimating equations.
analysis.main_results: Overall adjusted VE against RSV-related LRTD hospitalization/ED visits was 80% (95% CI 68-87), 70% (95% CI 53-81), and 51% (95% CI -12-78) in the first, second, and third season after vaccination, respectively. Overall adjusted VE against RSV-related ARI hospitalization/ED visits was 81% (71-87), 64% (48-75), and 60% (15-81), respectively. Adjusted VE among non-immunocompromised individuals trended 4-7% higher than corresponding overall estimates.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Bivalent RSVpreF provides protection against RSV-related respiratory hospitalization/ED visits for at least three seasons after vaccination in this population of older adults with a high prevalence of comorbidities. Estimates in the third season for ARI were more definitive, while those for LRTD were imprecise due to limited event numbers.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This study suggests bivalent RSVpreF vaccination results in substantial individual and public health benefit. The findings may inform future vaccine development and public health strategies for RSV prevention in older adults.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is a retrospective test-negative case-control study, which may introduce bias. The evidence strength is moderate due to the imprecision of LRTD estimates in the third season and the potential for confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates the effectiveness of bivalent RSVpreF vaccine against RSV-related respiratory disease hospitalizations and emergency department visits in adults aged ≥60 years over three RSV seasons. The study is a retrospective test-negative case-control study conducted at Kaiser Permanente Southern California. It found that adjusted vaccine effectiveness (VE) against RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) was 80%, 70%, and 51% in the first, second, and third seasons, respectively, while VE against RSV-related acute respiratory illness (ARI) was 81%, 64%, and 60%. The effectiveness was slightly higher among non-immunocompromised individuals. The authors concluded that the vaccine provides protection for at least three seasons, with more definitive results for ARI than for LRTD. The study's limitations include potential bias and imprecision in LRTD estimates, resulting in a moderate evidence strength assessment.

title: Computational designing of multiepitope based vaccine (MEBV) candidate against human metapneumovirus (HMPV) using immunoinformatics approach

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to design a multiepitope based vaccine (MEBV) candidate against human metapneumovirus (HMPV) using immunoinformatics approach, as HMPV is a respiratory pathogen closely related to respiratory syncytial virus and causes flu-like symptoms with potential for serious airway damage.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved computational designing of a vaccine candidate against HMPV, focusing on antigenic proteins and their interactions with immune cells. The research was conducted using immunoinformatics methods and targeted the development of a vaccine for HMPV.
analysis.methods: The researchers used computational methods to screen three antigenic proteins from HMPV, identified epitopes for T and B cell responses, combined them with linkers and beta-defensin as an adjuvant, and performed molecular docking and MD simulations to assess interactions with human TLR3.
analysis.main_results: The MEBV candidate was composed of 13 MHC-I epitopes, one MHC-II epitope, and four linear B-cell epitopes, resulting in a 296-amino-acid construct with an antigenicity score of 0.6644. Molecular docking and MD simulations showed a high degree of interaction with human TLR3, with binding energy of −14.6 and immune activation.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that the proposed MEBV has potential as an immunogen for HMPV, offering a novel approach to vaccine development through immunoinformatics.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide a foundation for further research into HMPV vaccine development, which could lead to improved surveillance, diagnosis, and prevention strategies for HMPV-related respiratory infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to computational methods and does not include experimental validation, which may affect the strength of the evidence. However, the use of molecular docking and MD simulations provides a moderate level of confidence in the vaccine's potential.

analysis.summary_en: This study presents a computational approach to designing a multiepitope based vaccine (MEBV) candidate against human metapneumovirus (HMPV). HMPV, a paramyxoviridae family respiratory pathogen, causes flu-like symptoms and can lead to serious airway damage, yet no vaccine exists. The researchers identified three antigenic proteins from HMPV and screened them for epitopes that could elicit immune responses. These epitopes were combined with linkers and beta-defensin as an adjuvant to create a 296-amino-acid MEBV with an antigenicity score of 0.6644. Molecular docking and MD simulations demonstrated a high degree of interaction with human TLR3, with binding energy of −14.6 and immune activation. Disulfide engineering was used to enhance construct stability, and cloning and codon optimization were performed to verify efficient expression in the target host. The findings suggest that the proposed MEBV has potential as an immunogen for HMPV, offering a novel approach to vaccine development. The study's results could inform future research into HMPV vaccine development, potentially improving surveillance, diagnosis, and prevention strategies. However, the study is limited to computational methods and lacks experimental validation, which may affect the strength of the evidence, though the use of molecular docking and MD simulations provides a moderate level of confidence.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) is a major cause of acute respiratory infections in children, but comprehensive data from sentinel surveillance in the post‐pandemic period remain limited. Understanding its epidemiology and co‐infection patterns is critical for surveillance and prevention.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We analyzed 36,143 respiratory specimens from ILI/SARI patients in Henan, China (2024–2025) using multiplex PCR for HMPV and 14 other pathogens. Overall HMPV positivity was 3.96% (1,432/36,143), with a sharp inter-year difference: 7.1% in 2024 vs. 1.7% in 2025, peaking at 26.2% during week 48.
analysis.methods: Positivity rates, enrichment ratios, co‐infection patterns, pathogen associations (OR/PR), and temporal dynamics (cross‐correlation and regression) were assessed. Children aged 3–5 years had the highest positivity (8.6%; enrichment ratio 2.18).
analysis.main_results: HMPV showed positive associations with Streptococcus pneumoniae (OR = 2.01) and Haemophilus influenzae (OR = 1.47), but negative associations with influenza virus (OR = 0.20) and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) (OR = 0.17). RSV positivity at a 1-week lag had a positive effect on HMPV (β = 0.15, P = 0.048).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The temporal lead‐lag relationship with RSV underscores the need for integrated surveillance and age‐targeted prevention. The marked 2024 resurgence warrants continued monitoring to determine whether the observed patterns represent a short‐term anomaly or a sustained change in HMPV circulation.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the importance of integrated surveillance systems to monitor HMPV and its co-infections, particularly with bacterial pathogens, and suggest the need for age-specific prevention strategies. The study also emphasizes the necessity of continued monitoring to understand long-term trends in HMPV circulation.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on sentinel surveillance data from a single geographic region, which may affect generalisability. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational nature of the study and potential confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the epidemiology, co-infections, and temporal dynamics of human metapneumovirus (HMPV) in Henan, China, during 2024–2025. It reports that HMPV positivity was 3.96% overall, with a notable resurgence in 2024. The virus showed positive associations with Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, but negative associations with influenza virus and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). RSV positivity at a 1-week lag had a positive effect on HMPV. The study highlights the need for integrated surveillance and age-targeted prevention strategies, as well as continued monitoring to determine whether the observed patterns represent a short-term anomaly or a sustained change in HMPV circulation. The findings are of moderate strength due to the observational design and potential confounding factors.

title: Reduced expression of human metapneumovirus matrix protein impacts virus assembly and ribonucleoprotein localization

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the various functions of the matrix (M) protein of human metapneumovirus (HMPV) to better understand its role in virus assembly and budding, given that other functions of the HMPV M protein have yet to be elucidated.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used a peptide-conjugated phosphorodiamidate morpholino oligomer (PPMO) antisense agent designed to block translation of the M gene during HMPV infection in cells.
analysis.methods: The researchers used a PPMO M to target and reduce M protein expression, and then analyzed the effects on virus production, viral titers, and viral ribonucleoprotein (vRNP) localization using techniques such as fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH).
analysis.main_results: Reductions in M protein expression led to dose-dependent decreases in M protein levels, with a 10 μM PPMO M treatment at 1 hour post-infection (hpi) resulting in a >95% reduction in M protein at 24 hpi. This reduction had a significant impact on virus production and titers, with increased inclusion body (IB) count per cell and decreased average IB volume per cell at 12 and 24 hpi. Additionally, there was a decrease in phosphoprotein (P) at the plasma membrane, but no change in vRNP movement.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study supports a model where the M protein is critical for the transfer to and stable association of vRNPs with the assembly sites at the membrane, rather than facilitating movement, and highlights the importance of M protein in virus assembly and budding.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that targeting the M protein could be a potential therapeutic approach for HMPV, as it significantly impacts virus production and titers, which could inform future treatment strategies for HMPV infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the use of a cell culture model, which may not fully represent the complexity of in vivo infections. The evidence strength is moderate due to the reliance on a single model system.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the role of the matrix (M) protein in human metapneumovirus (HMPV) assembly and budding by using a PPMO M to reduce M protein expression. The results showed that M protein is critical for vRNP localization at the membrane and significantly impacts virus production, suggesting potential therapeutic targets.

title: Emerging Trends in the Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Management of Human Metapneumovirus-Associated Respiratory Infections

analysis.scope_and_question: Human Metapneumovirus is a significant respiratory pathogen causing infections across all age groups, particularly in young children, immunocompromised individuals, and the elderly.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A systematic literature review was conducted using peer-reviewed journals, clinical trials, and recent studies focusing on Human Metapneumovirus infection. Data were extracted and analyzed to evaluate the effectiveness of antiviral therapies, monoclonal antibodies, immunomodulators, and vaccine candidates.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Studies indicate that Human Metapneumovirus primarily targets the respiratory epithelium, triggering immune responses that contribute to both viral clearance and disease pathogenesis. Investigational therapies, including fusion inhibitors and protease inhibitors, show promise but require further validation. Advances in vaccine development are ongoing, with several candidates in preclinical and early clinical stages. Human Metapneumovirus continues to pose a public health challenge due to the lack of targeted treatments and vaccines. Ongoing research into antiviral agents, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines is critical for effective disease management.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Immunomodulatory agents and herbal remedies may offer supportive benefits, but their efficacy against Human Metapneumovirus remains unproven. The virus evades immune responses via multiple mechanisms, contributing to disease severity, particularly in vulnerable populations. Further clinical trials are needed to establish safe and effective therapeutic options.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Improved diagnostic access, public awareness, and targeted research are essential for controlling HMPV infections.

analysis.summary_en: This review focuses on Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV) as a significant respiratory pathogen affecting all age groups, especially young children, immunocompromised individuals, and the elderly. The evidence base includes a systematic literature review of peer-reviewed journals, clinical trials, and recent studies. Key conclusions highlight that HMPV primarily targets the respiratory epithelium, triggering immune responses that influence both viral clearance and disease progression. Investigational therapies, such as fusion and protease inhibitors, show promise but require further validation. Vaccine development is ongoing, with several candidates in preclinical and early clinical stages. The virus's ability to evade immune responses contributes to disease severity in vulnerable populations. The review identifies the need for improved diagnostics, public awareness, and targeted research to manage HMPV infections effectively. Controversies include the unproven efficacy of immunomodulatory agents and herbal remedies, and the necessity for more clinical trials to establish safe and effective therapeutic options. Research and practice implications emphasize the importance of continued investigation into antiviral agents, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines to address the public health challenge posed by HMPV.

title: Age-stratified clinical features and factors associated with severe pneumonia in hospitalized children with human metapneumovirus–associated lower respiratory tract infection

analysis.research_question_and_background: Human metapneumovirus (hMPV) is a major cause of lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) in children, yet age-stratified analyses across the full pediatric age range and the associations between pathogen co-detection and disease severity remain incompletely characterized.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective study included children aged 0 to 6 years had the highest proportions of atelectasis (22.4%), unilateral involvement (65.7%), and severe pneumonia (31.0%).
analysis.methods: This study used a primary model to analyze associations between clinical features and severe pneumonia, incorporating factors such as atelectasis, underlying disease, consolidation, fever, wheezing, co-detection of Mycoplasma pneumoniae, absolute neutrophil counts, and C-reactive protein levels.
analysis.main_results: In the primary model, atelectasis (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 47.52), underlying disease (9.49), consolidation (6.82), fever (3.29), wheezing (2.50), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP) co-detection (1.90), higher absolute neutrophil counts (1.47 per 5 × 109/L), and higher C-reactive protein levels (1.14 per 10 mg/L) were associated with higher odds; higher absolute monocyte counts (0.71 per 1 × 109/L) and bacterial co-detection (0.60) were associated with lower odds.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: MP co-detection was more frequent in older children and was associated with higher odds of severe pneumonia after multivariable adjustment.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings may inform age-specific clinical assessment, with attention to respiratory status in young infants and, in school-aged children, peri-admission chest imaging when clinically indicated and further clinical and microbiological evaluation when MP is co-detected.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The overall age-group term did not reach statistical significance.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to delineate the age-related clinical features of human metapneumovirus (hMPV)-associated lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) and identify factors associated with severe pneumonia. A retrospective analysis of children aged 0 to 6 years revealed that atelectasis, underlying disease, consolidation, fever, wheezing, and co-detection of Mycoplasma pneumoniae were linked to higher odds of severe pneumonia. The frequency of MP co-detection increased with age, and it was associated with higher odds of severe pneumonia after multivariable adjustment. The study highlights the importance of age-specific clinical assessment, particularly focusing on respiratory status in young infants and chest imaging in older children. However, the overall age-group term did not reach statistical significance, indicating potential limitations in the generalizability of the findings. The results may inform targeted clinical practices and further research into hMPV and its interactions with other pathogens.

title: Immunoinformatics-guided design and in silico evaluation of BAFF- and APRIL-adjuvanted multi-epitope vaccine candidates against human metapneumovirus

analysis.research_question_and_background: Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) is a leading cause of acute respiratory tract infections in infants, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals; however, no licensed vaccine is currently available.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study employed an immunoinformatics-guided reverse vaccinology approach to design novel BAFF- and APRIL-adjuvanted multi-epitope vaccine candidates against HMPV.
analysis.methods: Major structural and non-structural HMPV proteins, including fusion (F), attachment glycoprotein (G), (matrix) M2-1, M2-2, phosphoprotein (P), nucleoprotein (N), small hydrophobic (SH), and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (L) proteins, were screened for antigenicity.
analysis.main_results: The final vaccine constructs contained 24 selected epitopes (8 CTL, 8 HTL, and 8 B-cell epitopes) and demonstrated favorable predicted antigenicity, stability, hydrophilicity, thermostability, and non-allergenic and non-toxic properties.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings suggest structural compatibility between the vaccine constructs and the selected TLRs; however, functional receptor binding and activation require experimental validation.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These computational findings provide a basis for prioritizing candidate constructs that may inform future experimental investigations into vaccine development for HMPV.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Molecular dynamics simulations and in vitro and in vivo studies are required to validate the structural stability, immunogenicity, safety, and protective efficacy of the proposed vaccine candidates.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to address the lack of a licensed vaccine for human metapneumovirus (HMPV) by employing an immunoinformatics-guided reverse vaccinology approach. The researchers identified and assembled 24 epitopes from major HMPV proteins into multi-epitope constructs, which were evaluated for antigenicity, stability, hydrophilicity, thermostability, and non-allergenic and non-toxic properties. The results indicated favorable predicted characteristics of the vaccine constructs, suggesting structural compatibility with Toll-like receptors TLR1 and TLR4. However, the authors emphasized that functional receptor binding and activation require experimental validation. The study's computational findings offer a foundation for further experimental investigation into vaccine development for HMPV. While the in silico approach provides valuable insights, additional studies are necessary to confirm the constructs' immunogenicity, safety, and protective efficacy. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the reliance on computational models without experimental validation.

title: Retrospective analysis of multiplex panel tests in the diagnosis of respiratory tract infections

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory tract infections (RTIs) remain a major global health concern, particularly in children.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective single-center study investigated the epidemiology of respiratory pathogens detected by mPCR, focusing on their distribution, age-related patterns, seasonal variation, and coinfections.
analysis.methods: Nasopharyngeal swab samples from 328 patients with suspected acute RTIs, collected between January 2022 and December 2023, were analyzed using the BioFire FilmArray Respiratory Panel 2.1.
analysis.main_results: At least one respiratory pathogen was detected in 270 of 328 specimens, yielding an overall positivity rate of 82.3%.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The vast majority of specimens (91.5%) were from pediatric patients (0–18 years).
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: mPCR demonstrated high diagnostic value, with pathogens detected in 82.3% of samples, predominantly viral agents.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted a retrospective analysis of multiplex PCR (mPCR) tests for respiratory tract infections (RTIs) in a single-center setting. The research aimed to evaluate the epidemiology of respiratory pathogens, including their distribution, age-related patterns, seasonal variation, and coinfections. The study analyzed 328 nasopharyngeal swab samples collected between January 2022 and December 2023 using the BioFire FilmArray Respiratory Panel 2.1. The results showed that 82.3% of specimens tested positive for at least one respiratory pathogen, with viral agents being the most frequently identified. The majority of cases were from pediatric patients, and coinfections were common, particularly involving adenovirus and human rhinovirus/enterovirus. The findings highlight the diagnostic utility of mPCR in identifying viral pathogens, which can support more informed clinical decision-making. However, the study did not evaluate antibiotic utilization, which limits its ability to fully address antimicrobial stewardship implications.

title: Post-pandemic re-establishment of respiratory virus seasonality and molecular epidemiology of Rhinovirus/Enterovirus in Northern Italy: a three-year surveillance study (2023-2026).

analysis.research_question_and_background: Following the COVID-19 pandemic, respiratory virus circulation progressively returned towards patterns observed in the pre-pandemic period. However, long-term epidemiological data describing the re-establishment of respiratory viral seasonality and the molecular diversity of Rhinovirus/Enterovirus (RV/EV) remain limited.
analysis.study_design_and_population: To investigate the circulation patterns of respiratory viruses and characterize the RV/EV in Northern Italy, a retrospective observational study was conducted on samples collected between April 2023 and April 2026 at Brescia Civic Hospital.
analysis.methods: Respiratory viruses were detected by real-time PCR, and RV/EV-positive samples were characterized through next-generation sequencing.
analysis.main_results: A total of 6,919 respiratory virus-positive samples were identified. SARS-CoV-2 remained the most frequently detected pathogen, followed by RV/EV, influenza A/B (FLU A/B), adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), parainfluenza virus, bocavirus, and human metapneumovirus. Distinct seasonal peaks were observed for FLU A/B and RSV during winter months, whereas RV/EV circulated continuously throughout the year. Molecular characterization of 224 RV/EV-positive samples revealed substantial genetic diversity. Pediatric patients accounted for the majority of sequenced cases.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Three years after the end of the COVID-19 pandemic, respiratory viruses have re-established their characteristic seasonal circulation patterns. Nevertheless, RV/EV remain the dominant non-influenza respiratory pathogens and display considerable genetic heterogeneity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Continuous molecular surveillance is essential for early detection of emerging respiratory viral threats.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study design limitations include the retrospective nature of the study and the focus on a single hospital, which may limit generalizability. However, the substantial genetic diversity observed in RV/EV highlights the importance of ongoing surveillance.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated respiratory virus circulation in Northern Italy from 2023 to 2026, focusing on Rhinovirus/Enterovirus (RV/EV). Despite SARS-CoV-2 being the most common pathogen, RV/EV showed continuous circulation and substantial genetic diversity, emphasizing the need for ongoing surveillance.
